title: What if games became tiny AI models instead of massive installs? Tiny browser driving sim demo
author: moorish-prince
selftext:
Hey everyone,

Been prototyping an AI game engine direction where you can run interactive games directly in the browser with no download, no setup, and tiny model sizes.

This driving sim demo is only \~5MB and runs instantly, but the bigger idea is complex 3D games and simulations becoming streamable, portable, and AI-generated instead of requiring massive installs and heavy engines underneath.

Feels like there’s an interesting future here for instant games, adaptive worlds, browser-native 3D, and AI-generated gameplay systems.

Would people here want to push this further? Port other games into this style? Explore AI-native game engines?

https://reddit.com/link/1tg7brj/video/ek9d22szns1h1/player

Demo:

[https://drift-sim-production.up.railway.app/](https://drift-sim-production.up.railway.app/)

comments.author: florodude
comments.body: Maybe for some genres but we will never move to completely ai powered games the same way that TV didn't kill books or plays

replies.author: moorish-prince
replies.body:
Yeah I don’t think AI games “replace games” either tbh. I think it’s more comparable to emulation, procedural generation, streaming, demakes, or neural rendering.

The interesting part to me is less “AI replaces devs” and more:  
can parts of game simulation become compressed/generated enough that complex interactive worlds become portable, streamable, or instantly playable in-browser?

More like how emulators, browser games, voxel engines, or procedural generation expanded what games could be and where they could run, not replacing the medium itself.

replies.author: moorish-prince
replies.body:
I don’t really see it as “hallucination replacing games,” more like a new compression/runtime layer.

Like:

\- instantly trying game demos in browser

\- running heavy games on lightweight hardware

\- shipping interactive worlds as tiny packages instead of 150GB installs

\- portable simulations that run anywhere

More similar to streaming, emulation, procedural generation, or DLSS than replacing traditional games entirely.

replies.author: moorish-prince
replies.body:
The Minecraft browser example isn’t really the same thing, that’s still a traditional game/web client trying to explicitly run normal game systems in-browser. This is a learned simulator: a tiny neural model approximating the behavior of the environment itself.

MY implementation is more lightweight and requires less compute, that’s literally the whole point of the experiment. The demo on OP is a playable driving sim inspired by games/sims that are normally massive installs, compressed into a \~5MB model running locally in-browser. You don’t get the full exact original game, you get a lightweight playable approximation/slice.

The intuition is similar to compression. A video file is smaller than storing every raw frame individually because it learns patterns and predicts changes. A learned simulator can sometimes do something similar for interactive environments: instead of storing full assets, physics systems, maps, etc, the model learns the patterns of “what usually happens next” from gameplay data.
